1    A. Legal Standard                                                       
2       When a defendant moves for dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction 

3  pursuant to Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(2), it is the plaintiff who “bears the burden of 
4  demonstrating that jurisdiction is appropriate.”  Schwarzenegger v. Fred Martin 
5  Motor Co., 374 F.3d 797, 800 (9th Cir. 2004) (citation omitted).  When the 

6  defendant’s motion to dismiss relies only on written materials, “the plaintiff need 
7  only make a prima facie showing of jurisdictional facts.”  Id. (quotation and 
8  citation omitted).  The court must determine whether a plaintiff’s “pleadings and 
9  affidavits establish” the requisite showing.  Data Disc, Inc. v. Sys. Tech. Assocs., 

10  557 F.2d 1280, 1286 (9th Cir. 1977).  “The plaintiff cannot ‘simply rest on the bare 
11  allegations of its complaint,’ but uncontroverted allegations in the complaint must 
12  be taken as true.”  Mavrix Photo, Inc. v. Brand Techs., Inc., 647 F.3d 1218, 1223 

13  (9th Cir. 2011) (quoting Schwarzenegger, 374 F.3d at 800).  If any conflict exists 
14  between the parties’ evidence, the court must resolve it in the plaintiff’s favor. 
15  AT&T v. Compagnie Bruxelles Lambert, 94 F.3d 586, 588 (9th Cir. 1996).    
16       A federal district court sitting in diversity may exercise personal jurisdiction 

17  “to the extent the forum state’s laws constitutionally provide.”  Metro. Life Ins. Co. 
18  v. Neaves, 912 F.2d 1062, 1065 (9th Cir. 1990).  Washington’s long-arm statute 
19  authorizes courts to exercise jurisdiction over nonresident defendants to the “full 

20  extent” of the Due Process Clause.  Easter v. Am. W. Fin., 381 F.3d 948, 960 (9th 
1  Cir. 2004) (citing Shute v. Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc., 783 P.2d 78, 79-80 (Wash. 
2  1989)); see also Corker v. Costco Wholesale Corp., 585 F. Supp. 3d 1284, 1290 

3  (W.D. Wash. 2022).  Accordingly, the Court need only determine whether    
4  exercising personal jurisdiction in this case comports with due process.  See 
5  Yamashita v. LG Chem, Ltd., 62 F.4th 496, 502 (9th Cir. 2023).  Due process 

6  requires that the defendant have “certain minimum contacts” with a forum state 
7  “such that the maintenance of the suit does not offend ‘traditional notions of fair 
8  play and substantial justice.’”  Int’l Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310, 316 
9  (1945) (quoting Milliken v. Meyer, 311 U.S. 457, 463 (1940)).             

10       The Supreme Court has recognized two kinds of personal jurisdiction: 
11  general and specific.  Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown, 564 U.S. 
12  915, 919 (2011) (citing Helicopteros Nacionales de Colombia, S.A. v. Hall, 466 

13  U.S. 408, 414, nn.8 & 9 (1984)).  Arxada, LLC argues that the Court lacks a proper 
14  basis to exercise either general or specific jurisdiction.  Plaintiffs assert only that 
15  the evidence demonstrates “a prima facie case of general jurisdiction,” without 
16  contesting Arxada, LLC’s denial of specific jurisdiction.  ECF No. 11 at 2 

17  (emphasis added).  Thus, Plaintiff has waived any argument that the Court has 
18  specific jurisdiction.  See Shakur v. Schriro, 514 F.3d 878, 892 (9th Cir. 2008) 
19  (plaintiff waived argument by failing to raise it in opposition to a motion to 

20  dismiss).

14    C. General Jurisdiction                                                 
15       “Two authorities govern a federal court’s exercise of personal jurisdiction 
16  over a defendant: the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause and the long 

17  arm statute of the state in which the district court sits.”  Briskin v. Shopify, Inc., 87 
18  F.4th 404, 411 (9th Cir. 2023).  The Ninth Circuit has interpreted Washington’s 
19  long-arm statute, RCW 4.28.185, to “permit[] the exercise of jurisdiction to the full 

20  extent of the due process clause.”  Easter v. Am. W. Fin., 381 F.3d 948, 960 (9th 
1  Cir. 2004) (citation omitted); see also Failla v. FixtureOne Corp., 336 P.3d 1112, 
2  1116 (Wash. 2014) (en banc) (noting that Washington’s long-arm statute is 

3  “designed to be coextensive with federal due process”).                   
4       “A court may exercise general jurisdiction ‘only when a defendant is 
5  essentially at home in the state.’”  Impossible Foods, Inc. v. Impossible X LLC, 80 

6  F.4th 1079, 1086 (9th Cir. 2023) (quoting Ford Motor Co. v. Mont. Eighth Jud. 
7  Dist. Ct., 141 S. Ct. 1017, 1024 (2021)).  The inquiry is whether a foreign 
8  “corporation’s affiliations with the State are so continuous and systematic as to 
9  render it essentially at home in the forum State.”  Daimler AG v. Bauman, 571 U.S. 

10  117, 138-39 (2014) (citation, quotation marks, and alteration omitted).  “The 
11  paradigm all-purpose forums for general jurisdiction are a corporation’s place of 
12  incorporation and principal place of business.”  Id. at 118 (citing Goodyear Dunlop 

13  Tires, 564 U.S. at 924).  However, “in an ‘exceptional case,’ a corporate 
14  defendant’s operations in another forum ‘may be so substantial and of such a 
15  nature as to render the corporation at home in that state.’”  BNSF Ry. Co. v. Tyrrell, 
16  581 U.S. 402, 413 (2017) (quoting Daimler, 571 U.S. at 139 n.19).  This is a high 

17  standard—for example, in BNSF Ry. Co., the Supreme Court held there was no 
18  general jurisdiction even though the defendant had more than 2,000 miles of 
19  railroad track and employed more than 2,000 employees in the forum state.  Id. at 

20  414.  The standard is so particular because it opens the defendant to suit on causes 
1  of action that are unrelated to their activities in the forum state.  King v. Am. 
2  Family Mut. Ins. Co., 632 F.3d 570, 579 (9th Cir. 2011).                  

3       There is no basis for the Court to find general jurisdiction exists.  The 
4  Complaint states that Arxada, LLC is organized under the laws of Delaware and 
5  does not specify a principal place of business.  ECF No. 4 at 3.  Plaintiffs do not 

6  dispute Arxada, LLC’s representation that its principal place of business is in New 
7  Jersey.  ECF No. 1 at 4; ECF No. 2 at 2; ECF No. 15 at 4.                 
8       Nor have Plaintiffs established that this is an “exceptional case” for 
9  extending general jurisdiction beyond the paradigmatic bases.  Besides contending 

10  that Arxada, LLC purchased, supervises, and manages Enviro Tech (an allegation 
11  that is contradicted by Plaintiffs’ own supporting materials, ECF No. 13-1), the

14  constitutes an “exceptional case” to extend general jurisdiction outside the 
15  paradigm forums.  ECF No. 4 at 4; see BNSF Ry., 581 U.S. at 413.  In response, 
16  Plaintiffs offer further arguments regarding Arxada, LLC’s contacts with  

17  Washington.4  But the evidence before the Court ultimately shows little, if any,

20       Last, Plaintiffs cite to the purchase agreement and the stock purchase

6  Arxada entity it pertains to, or strongly indicates that it pertains to Arxada AG.  
7  The fact that there is a relationship between Arxada, LLC and the other Arxada 
8  entities “is insufficient, on its own, to justify imputing” the other Arxada entities’ 
9  contacts with Washington to Arxada, LLC, “for the purpose of establishing 

10  personal jurisdiction.”  See Ranza v. Nike, Inc., 793 F.3d 1059, 1070 (9th Cir. 
11  2015).  But even if Plaintiffs had shown that all the above contacts were 
12  attributable to Arxada, LLC, it would not amount to an “exceptional case” to 

13  extend general jurisdiction beyond its paradigmatic bases.  See BNSF Ry. Co., 581 
14  U.S. at 413.                                                              
15       In short, the record reflects that general jurisdiction over Arxada, LLC 
16  would be proper in Delaware or New Jersey and possibly other jurisdictions, but 

17  not Washington.  Plaintiffs have failed to demonstrate a prima facie case of general 
18  jurisdiction.

1    D. Jurisdictional Discovery                                             
2       Plaintiffs ask this Court to permit jurisdictional discovery to enable Plaintiffs 

3  to provide “further evidence that Arxada is doing business in Washington.”  ECF 
4  No. 10 at 10.                                                             
5       “Jurisdictional discovery ‘should ordinarily be granted where pertinent facts 

6  bearing on the question of jurisdiction are controverted or where a more  
7  satisfactory showing of the facts is necessary.’”  LNS Enters. LLC v. Cont'l Motors, 
8  Inc., 22 F.4th 852, 864 (9th Cir. 2022) (quoting Laub v. U.S. Dep't of Interior, 342 
9  F.3d 1080, 1093 (9th Cir. 2003)) (other citation and internal quotation marks 

10  omitted).  Jurisdictional discovery should not be granted, however, on a plaintiff’s 
11  “hunch that [such discovery] might yield jurisdictionally relevant facts,” Boschetto 
12  v. Hansing, 539 F.3d 1011, 1020 (9th Cir. 2008), or “bare allegations in the face of 

13  specific denials,” Terracom v. Valley Nat’l Bank, 49 F.3d 555, 562 (9th Cir. 1995) 
14  (citation omitted).                                                       
15       Here, Plaintiffs have presented nothing beyond a mere hunch that discovery 
16  might yield jurisdictionally relevant facts.  The materials Plaintiffs have submitted 

17  to date only further demonstrate that this Court cannot exercise general jurisdiction 
18  over Arxada, LLC.  The Court is unpersuaded that jurisdictional discovery would 
19  yield facts sufficient to make this an exceptional case to extend general jurisdiction 

20

2  denied.

8    A. Legal Standard                                                       
9       To survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss, a complaint must contain 

10  sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to “state a claim to relief that is plausible 
11  on its face.”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009).  “Threadbare recitals of 
12  the elements of a cause of action, supported by mere conclusory statements, do not 

13  suffice.”  Id.  In considering a motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim, the

11    B. Good Faith and Fair Dealing                                          
12       The Complaint alleges that Defendant Enviro Tech breached the covenant of 

13  good faith and fair dealing by (1) failing to pay Plaintiffs one-third of the net sale 
14  proceeds owed to them; (2) failing to repay Plaintiff Erickson’s capital  
15  contribution; (3) refusing to provide an accounting of the partnership assets; and

19  specific term or obligation of the alleged partnership agreement to which the 

20  implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing was attached.  ECF No. 9 at 6-7.  
1  “Every contract imposes upon each party a duty of good faith and fair dealing in its

19    F. Leave to Amend                                                       

20       Enviro Tech requests dismissal with prejudice.  ECF No. 9 at 14.  Plaintiffs 
1  request leave to amend if the Court grants Enviro Tech’s Motion to Dismiss, citing 
2  the “liberal construction of Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(2).”  ECF No. 10 at 10.   

3       Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(2) provides that a court should freely grant leave to 
4  amend the pleadings when justice so requires.  “Amendments to pleadings are 
5  ‘applied with extreme liberality.’”  Key Tronic Corp. v. SkyBell Techs., Inc., No. 

6  23-CV-237,
2023 WL 8634781
, at *1 (E.D. Wash. Dec. 13, 2023) (quoting Owens 
7  v. Kaiser Found. Health Plan, Inc.,
244 F.3d 708, 712
 (9th Cir. 2001)).  Courts 
8  consider five factors when deciding whether to grant leave to amend: (1) bad faith, 
9  (2) undue delay, (3) prejudice to the opposing party, (4) previous amendments, and 

10  (5) futility of the amendment.  Forman v. Davis,
371 U.S. 178, 182
 (1962); see 
11  also United States v. Corinthian Colls.,
655 F.3d 984, 995
 (9th Cir. 2011).  “[T]he 
12  court must grant all inferences in favor of allowing amendment.”  Griggs v. Pace 

13  Am. Grp., Inc.,
170 F.3d 877
, 880 (9th Cir. 1999).                        
14       On balance, the Davis factors weigh against leave to amend as to the breach 
15  of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing and conversion claims.  
16  Although there is no indication of bad faith, Plaintiffs have amended the pleadings 

17  once, after removal and before any defendant filed a responsive pleading or motion 
18  to dismiss.  Finally, the Court finds that the Court finds amendment would be futile 
19  as it does not appear that Plaintiffs will be able to cure the deficiencies in the 

20  claims.  See ECF No. 9 at 8-9, 14.  As to the Bac Stop and OC3 claims, Enviro 
1  Tech has not demonstrated how amendment would be futile.  Thus, the factors 
2  weigh in favor of leave to amend as to the Bac Stop and OC3 claims.
